title: Will Michael Carrick be Manchester United’s permanent coach? Exploring the key questions
content:
Michael Carrick’s January appointment as Manchester United’s interim head coach has undoubtedly improved the club’s season but will it end with him being placed in permanent charge?

The Athletic’s Mark Critchley has spoken to multiple people about the situation over the past week and here, with the help of colleagues Ahmed Walid, Andy Mitten, Carl Anka and Chris Weatherspoon, he explores the key questions that will decide what happens next at Old Trafford.

These include what United executives and players are thinking, what Carrick has shown on and off the field over the past two months and whether, ultimately, he wants the job full-time.

Results have been better than anyone could realistically have expected: Carrick’s eight games in charge have brought six wins, a draw and just a single defeat.

Even after losing at Newcastle in their most recent match on Wednesday, United sit top of the post-Carrick appointment league table by two points.

The performances have not always been flawless, and have tailed off since a remarkable pair of opening wins against Manchester City and Arsenal, but the improvement compared to predecessor Ruben Amorim’s final days in charge is unquestionable.

United were seventh in the actual table at the time of Carrick’s appointment, nine points adrift of third-place Aston Villa. Now they are third, level on points with but ahead of Villa courtesy of a superior, and much-improved, goal difference.

Qualifying for the Europa League was the target at the start of the season after a miserable 15th-place finish last term. Expectations have been raised since, though.

Director of football Jason Wilcox set a return to the Champions League as the goal for the remainder of the campaign in a meeting with the first-team squad on the morning of Amorim’s January 5 dismissal.

Carrick has given himself every chance of clearing that higher bar over the final nine games. United lead a pack of four clubs chasing the top-five finish that should bring Champions League qualification, and given they do not have the parallel European commitments of their immediate rivals, they should be considered favourites.

Mark Critchley

Carrick won the battle to be Amorim’s immediate successor because the United hierarchy viewed him as an impressive coach whose familiarity with the squad and the club’s inner workings from his previous spells with them as a player and coach would not leave him overawed by the task at hand.

United’s confidence in Carrick’s ability has been vindicated, and Old Trafford’s key decision-makers are predictably pleased with the job he has done so far.

Yet as happy as United are with their choice of coach until the end of this season, they insist that they will not rush into appointing Amorim’s permanent successor.

The intention has always been to carry out a thorough process when selecting the first team’s next leader and, though that will run in tandem with the race for a place in the Champions League over the coming months, the club do not expect to finalise a decision before the end of the season.

Naturally, the positive results over the past eight games have only helped Carrick’s chances of getting the job permanently, but how United fare over these nine remaining Premier League fixtures will have just as much of a bearing.

Mark Critchley

It is not uncommon for a newly-installed manager or head coach, whether arriving on a permanent or interim basis, to have an uplifting effect on a squad of players they inherit. Carrick’s appointment at United has been no different in that respect.

People close to the dressing room have praised his methods on the training pitches, believing that the players have benefited from his shorter but more concentrated and more intense sessions. The calibre of his backroom staff — particularly Steve Holland, the former England assistant manager — has also been praised.

By contrast, there were times when Amorim’s reliance on a group of coaches who were relatively inexperienced was questioned, although his loyalty to people he had worked with throughout his journey in Portuguese football was commendable.

Carrick’s communication is described as clear and constant. He has at times made a point of seeking out and speaking with players who are on the fringes of the squad and eager for more opportunities.

The coaching staff’s focus on small tactical and positional details has also been appreciated, as have one-to-one sessions with individuals, notably Travis Binnion’s work with striker Benjamin Sesko.

Bruno Fernandes’ form has hit new heights since being restored to his natural No 10 role under Carrick, with the United captain last month boiling the difference the former England midfielder has made down to one word: freedom.

“I think Michael came in with the right ideas of giving the players the responsibility, but also some freedom to take the responsibility on the pitch during the decisions that are needed,” Fernandes told UK broadcaster TNT Sports after last month’s 2-0 win against Tottenham Hotspur.

“He’s very good with words. I think he still remembers when I told him last time he was our manager (a previous spell as interim coach in 2021, before leaving for a near three-year stint as manager of Championship side Middlesbrough), for our last game, and I was sure Michael could be a great manager, and now he is showing it.”

Mark Critchley

Not everyone has been supportive of Carrick’s performance as coach, with Paul Scholes posting and then deleting a critical message about his former United and England midfield colleague on Instagram after the defeat by Newcastle. Another ex-team-mate, Gary Neville, has said that he is “not against” Carrick getting the job full-time but that United should “go for the best class of manager available”. Former United captain Roy Keane has also made his views clear, saying early in Carrick’s tenure that the club need a “bigger and better manager”.

But what do some of United’s less outspoken former players think? The Athletic spoke to Nemanja Vidic and Andy Cole to find out.

“Michael and the players have my support, and I hope they provide us with the Champions League football that United must have. That’s the aim for now. Let Michael and his players try and reach it. Don’t put pressure him as to what comes after. Let’s enjoy it for now,” says Vidic.

“Under Michael, I saw a reaction from the players, especially in the first few games. I was at the Manchester derby (United’s 2-0 home win in Carrick’s debut after replacing Amorim), with my friend Vladimir. I sat next to Sir Alex (Ferguson, the club’s legendary long-time manager) and it was wonderful to see him. Vladimir said it was the best day of his life, after the birth of his child! I’d not felt Old Trafford with that energy and passion for a long time.

“I saw energy, positivity in the football, players enjoying themselves more on the pitch. Yes, the Newcastle game was a bad one, and a bad result — (but) we all have them.

“Michael was a good team-mate who tried to control his emotions and think clearly. He has his own opinions but doesn’t push to tell it if nobody asks. But he has a side where he has a strong opinion on how he sees football. He’s not necessarily loud, a screamer or a shouter, someone who says that he’s the cleverest in the room, but he’s a strong character, and he needs to be. But forget the future for now, enjoy the present.”

Cole also praised Carrick’s calmness: “Michael is a very understated individual, a cool, quiet, down-to-earth guy. The way he played was understated. He had a lot of quality but was never given the praise for that quality. He’s brought a calmness into the dressing room, told players to express themselves and enjoy it.

“I’m not saying every game has been perfect, but it’s about winning, and that’s what United have done (under him). The City game was a dream. Everyone expected United to get pumped, same with the Arsenal game (a 3-2 away win against the current league leaders the following weekend). He won both and played good football, too.

“Michael understands what the club is about. He’s also benefited from one game most weeks (with United not playing in any of the UEFA competitions this season): that means fresher players, fewer injuries and more time with your players. But then, European football is a bonus, and that’s what you want. Manchester United should be in Europe every season. If he’s not fortunate enough to get the job full-time, I don’t think he’ll struggle to get another.”

Andy Mitten

Carrick and his staff have shown positive signs of understanding the tactical landscape of the Premier League and tailoring their ideas to the profiles of United’s current squad.

Since his first game, that 2-0 defeat of Manchester City in January, the team’s in-possession ideas have been on show, with the rotations of the front line being key to that result. Whether it’s in build-up, progression of the ball or attacking the final third, there’s a clarity in how the team has been operating in these phases.

One of United’s main ideas under Carrick has been the focus on central passing combinations, aided by the narrowness and flexibility of the forwards and captain Fernandes. This works in tandem with the extra responsibility given to the defenders to break the lines and find the front four in pockets of space or behind the opposition back line.

The passing combinations and fluidity of the forwards have also helped United attack the wide areas in threatening situations.

Defensively, the team’s organisation has looked solid in a mid- or low-block, but the high press has looked questionable and inconsistent in its effectiveness — an area of the game that Carrick, his staff and the players need to work on.

The continued focus on set pieces and addition to United’s strong base from earlier in the season is a credit to Carrick and his assistants, who are doubling down on one of the team’s current strengths.

When it comes to Carrick’s in-game tactical tweaks, it’s too early to judge, and in general, more time is needed to have a better assessment of him.

There’s another aspect as well. He is still learning on the job having had limited previous experience as a number one, and all coaches take time to develop.

Ahmed Walid

Carrick plays a straight bat to most questions, and especially those regarding potential signings, injured players’ lay-offs and, in particular, his long-term future at the club. When asked whether centre-back Harry Maguire was in the best form of his seven-season United career, Carrick said “there is a case” for the argument, without making it clear whether he supported said case.

This guarded approach to his dealings with the media is in sharp contrast to Amorim, who would speak openly on all manner of subjects, and could be described by some as honest to a fault.

At times, that candidness caused issues, such as with his infamous “worst team in history” remark. Which is to say nothing of the incendiary post-match press conference following his final match in charge, against Leeds, which expedited his exit.

His replacement is not likely to rock the boat in the same way. Carrick the interviewee is much like Carrick the midfielder: understated and unlikely to draw headlines.

Carl Anka, Mark Critchley

The answer depends on who the favoured alternative is. If they’re jobless, the effective savings from keeping Carrick are lower. If they’re in a job elsewhere that United would need to extract them from, it’ll cost more.

Managerial transfer fees pale in comparison to those commanded when recruiting players but, like just about everything in football, they are growing more and more. United have experience of that: snaffling Amorim and his staff from Lisbon’s Sporting CP in November 2024 set them back £11million.

Of perhaps greater importance to the financial picture is how much it will cost to continue employing and, as is likely in football and certainly in recent times at United, eventually fire Carrick. Like player wages, manager/head coach salaries are never reliably disclosed, but it seems fair to suggest it would be less expensive for the club if he remained in the Old Trafford dugout than if they hired a more coveted, higher-profile figure.

Correspondingly, it would also cost less to dismiss him if things went south. Amorim and his coaching staff’s sacking in early January exposed United to a maximum settlement liability of £15.9million, to go alongside a swath of similar payments in recent years. Getting rid of Erik ten Hag cost £10.4m; Ole Gunnar Solskjaer’s dismissal three years earlier came with a bill of £9.1m; Jose Mourinho’s ousting in December 2018 saw them pay out £19.6m — the largest head coach settlement in club history.

In all, United’s 13-year post-Ferguson era has seen at least £65million in managerial payouts, and almost certainly a bit more beyond that. Hiring Carrick would, theoretically, keep any future such costs down, though basing a managerial choice on what the bill would be if the appointment fails probably isn’t in anyone’s business plan.

There are also the indirect costs of getting an appointment wrong. United declared record revenues in 2024-25 but, without European football, will see a drop this term, and have slumped from reliably being English football’s biggest revenue-generator to only the fourth-highest earning club.

With rivals growing, big transfer debts to pay and bank debt still costing around £40million a year, getting turnover moving in the right direction is key. Improving on the pitch is essential to that; Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal and Chelsea have all earned around £80m from this season’s Champions League, with more potentially to come from a prize pot United are currently unable to dip into.

Installing the correct head coach would make them more able to rely on big sums from UEFA’s flashiest club competition.

Chris Weatherspoon

United did not spend on the first team in the recent winter transfer window, making it clear they would only look to accelerate deals for players they already intended to sign come the summer if the opportunity to do so arose.

Central midfield has long been in need of strengthening and is expected to be a primary focus, with at least one required in the next transfer window to replace the departing Casemiro. United would ideally want an athletic, defensively-minded midfielder who can complement Kobbie Mainoo, while there may be scope for an additional midfield signing who can split playing time with the 20-year-old academy graduate.

Nottingham Forest’s Elliot Anderson is their first-choice target, while talks regarding the availability of Brighton & Hove Albion’s Carlos Baleba were held last summer via intermediaries.

United are also thought to have preliminary shortlists for a potential centre-back signing. Adding a left-back who can take over from Luke Shaw when needed and offer more width down that flank might also be smart.

Carl Anka and Mark Critchley

Carrick has been asked on countless occasions about his chances of taking the job permanently and, true to form, has given precious little away.

“It’s going to be every week, isn’t it, this?,” he joked in response to the latest inquiry, following the defeat of Crystal Palace last weekend. The substance of the answer that followed was no different from usual, though he did make clear that he is enjoying the role.

“I love being here. I love doing what I’m doing,” Carrick said. “Of course, winning games helps, and the boys are doing great with that. We’ll just have to see where it ends up. There’s not really much I can give you on top of that.”

Those who know Carrick well believe that he would be happy to continue as United’s head coach beyond the end of this season, provided that the position was right for him.

At the end of his first short-term managerial spell following Solskjaer’s sacking in 2021, Carrick brought his 15-year stay at Old Trafford to an end despite incoming interim manager Ralf Rangnick being keen to keep him on as part of his staff.

Carrick also spent time away from management after leaving Middlesbrough last summer and explored post-playing avenues in football, including appearances in the media on the BBC’s Match of the Day and Amazon Prime’s Champions League coverage. He is said to have enjoyed those experiences but said last week that, despite that, he still has the coaching bug.

“I never really lost it, to be honest, whether it’s managing, head coach, whatever role that is,” he said. “It comes down to working with players and people, really, to get the best out of people and backroom staff and supporters.”

Mark Critchley

The pool of coaching talent expected to be on the market come the end of the club season in May, or after the World Cup concludes in July, is a little shallower than it was upon Amorim’s dismissal.

Thomas Tuchel, who held talks with United’s hierarchy over succeeding Ten Hag in May 2024, would have been considered a viable candidate at that time but signed a two-year contract extension as England’s head coach last month. Carlo Ancelotti, another highly-experienced coach set to manage at this summer’s tournament, is set to remain in charge of Brazil’s national team until 2030. Julian Nagelsmann’s Germany contract commits him to that role until the end of the 2028 European Championship.

United’s hierarchy have historic interest in Roberto De Zerbi, who is currently clubless after leaving France’s Marseille last month. Like Tuchel, the former Brighton & Hove Albion head coach held advanced talks with United at the end of the 2023-24 season, only for Ten Hag to remain in post until the following October.

Andoni Iraola of Bournemouth, Crystal Palace’s Oliver Glasner and Marco Silva of Fulham are Premier League proven and are all approaching the end of their respective contracts, though those sides all currently sit in mid-table.
